reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript "Broadband acousto-optic modulators on Silicon Nitride" describes the development and implementation of a novel, traveling wave optically broadband acousto-optic modulator using thin silicon nitride waveguides. These modulators, capable of achieving a π/2 phase shift at a wavelength of 1550 nm, offer significant advantages due to their avoidance of complex fabrication processes and heterogeneous integration, capitalizing instead on ultra-low-loss waveguides to achieve long interaction lengths necessary for efficient modulation. The architecture utilizes spiraling waveguides that allow light to repeatedly pass through an acoustic field up to 38 times within a compact area, facilitating effective modulation with a Vπ of 8.98 V at 704 MHz and an insertion loss of just 1.13 dB. This manuscript also highlights the modulators' immediate applicability in optomechanical sensing systems. I recommend publication of this manuscript with a few minor comments:
1. In the abstract, “As silicon nitride has favorable optical properties, such as ultra-low-loss and a large optical transparency window, a rich ecosystem of potential photonic integrated circuits are therefore inhibited.” This sentence does not read well.
2. Figure 1, green, yellow, gray, materials not specified in figure or caption. From the text later one can sort of figure it out, but I recommend labeling those materials in the figure.
3. On phase matching, it mentions the basic idea of that in the text when introducing Figure 1e, and the results of increasing of numbers of loops in Figure 2. Could the author show more intermediate results in between of the design philosophy and final results? This is very important technical content for readers to understand, appreciate, and repeat the design.
4. The authors mention the loss of 1.1 dB is primarily because of metal layer; can they explain more how they reach this conclusion?
5. Could the authors provide more information regarding the material properties and method for AlN and Mo?
6. Could the authors comment on how to further how to further increase the acoustic-optical interaction in the future?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The article under review describes broadband acousto-optic modulators on silicon nitride. In this work, the authors utilize ultra-low loss thin silicon nitride (<100nm) to realize the modulators. The modulator design is optimized by maximizing the optical and acoustic interaction through the use of a long spiral. This device avails modulators to the SiN photonics toolkit. The manuscript is interesting and I recommend publishing the manuscript after addressing the following points:
1) Integrated photonics technologies have a variety of modulator types (eg. electro-optic, free-carrier based). The modulator described in this work uses the acousto-optic effect. A table which allows a comparison of modulator merics such as half wave voltage / bandwidth / loss/ foot print etc. should be added to the paper.
2) Currently, the half wave voltage in the paper is higher than other technologies. Can the authors discuss what can be done to reduce it? The interaction length through ultra-low loss silicon nitride requires a 26cm length. There should be a fundamental limit to how long the waveguide can be that is loss limited. Can the authors comment on whether increasing the length is a feasible approach to reduce Vpi
3) Within the context of comment (2), there should be a trade off with the modulator footprint which may be useful to discuss as well.
4) Other than in Fig. 8 (d), can the authors comment on whether any data averaging was done to obtain the plots in the article? If so, how did they decide on the number of measurements used for the averaging?
5) To further improve the transducer, a greater thickness is required. More commentary around potential design improvements to enhance the modulator performance is warranted given that LiNbO3 modulators are currently very competitive. For example (but not limited to these), can the overlap be improved, and if so how much, could any other material integration give better performance etc.
6) Though higher order acoustic modes may be advantageous, it is not clear how one can control which modes are excited. The authors should clarify this. If there is a difficulty in exciting a specific higher order mode and the design is typically optimized for a specific mode, then is there an inherent tradeoff?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, the authors demonstrate an acousto-optic phase modulator based on a spiral waveguide in thin-film silicon nitride, using travelling acoustic waves from IDTs on a Mo/AlN top layer. In contrast to prior work on silicon nitride, this modulator design does not use optical resonant enhancement, or suspended structures as in other recent work [31]. Using up to a 26 cm spiral waveguide, along with careful phase control over dozens of segments in the acoustic wave path, a V_pi of ~9 V is achieved for acousto-optic phase modulation at 704 MHz with ~1.1 dB insertion loss.
In general the work is interesting and seems technically to mostly be of high quality, except for a key issue addressed below. That aside, I am a bit uncertain if the manuscript represents the degree of novelty that the authors seem to claim, in part because the design is primarily based on principles that have already been reported in other recent work, and otherwise because I have some doubts about the applicability and practicality of using such a large structure and high RF power for producing phase modulation at a single RF frequency, particularly related to the next point:
Critically, I am not certain that I believe the authors' claim that the device is "broadband." It certainly is not broadband in the RF/acoustic sense, and I do not think it is broadband in the optical sense as well. When two (or more) modulators at the same frequency are placed in series, there can be constructive or destructive interference of the modulation index depending on the phase delay. The authors explore this in the supplement, and use this to design specific delay lengths between each segment. However I am not sure that their conclusion of the negligible impact of group index. Perhaps this can be true for operation around a certain theoretical design wavelength, but I do not see how this can produce broadband operation over 100+ nm. In any case, much more narrowband/continuous wavelength data would be needed to be provided to justify any claim about bandwidth.
I am not certain that the level of lithographic control to match phase delays to sub-radian levels over centimeter lengths is possible without post-fabrication trimming, due to variations in waveguide width and film stress and thickness across the wafer. However, perhaps given the weak confinement of thin silicon nitride waveguides and the use of a foundry process, this is possible in principle.
Even if constructive interference between all the segments is achieved, then it is still achieved for only certain wavelength bands due to material and waveguide dispersion. This is understood from basic modulator theory. If you have two modulators in series so that there is a phase difference theta between them:
phi(t) = beta*cos(omega*t) + beta*cos(omega*t+theta)
then this can be rewritten as
phi(t) = 2*beta*cos(theta/2)*cos(omega*t+theta/2).
If the phase theta is pi between the two modulation segments, then the modulation cancels. So, we want to keep theta to a multiple of 2*pi. This can be achieved, but it cannot be entirely "broadband" unless phi doesn't vary as a function of wavelength. I have a hard time believing that v_g varies so little over 100 nm that light does not accumulate an appreciable phase difference over tens of cm.
In the case of multiple segments, the interference becomes more complicated, but the principle is the same. Even with random phases between each segment, it should be possible to find "good" wavelengths where most of the interference is constructive. Conversely, there are "bad' wavelengths where most of the interference is destructive. This is already reported in detail in many papers, e.g. [33] and [37]. Another way of thinking about it is that, from the standpoint of light waves, experiencing many discrete modulation segments in series is not temporally very different from experiencing modulation at a discrete point in a resonator that it traverses numerous times, except that phase matching is more perfectly achieved for the latter via the resonance condition.
As far as I can tell, the only figure in the entire paper that is used to justify the claim of optical bandwidth is Fig. 2g, which shows modulation data at a series of coarse, discrete points across 100 nm. The same plot could be constructed from measurements of modulation in a resonator, as long as the laser was tuned to the resonant frequencies (equivalent to "good wavelengths" mentioned above). So in that sense the resonator approach would also seem to meet the authors' criterion for "broadband."
If the authors are not able to experimentally demonstrate broadband operation over a continuous wavelength band that contradicts this assessment, then the results of this paper are all a bit hard to interpret--since V_pi is going to vary as a function of wavelength, and the result of 9 V may occur only at certain magic wavelengths. I do think that the device may be able to achieve "broadband" operation over smaller continuous bands, but I believe that it cannot be continuously broadband over the 100 nm band shown in Fig. 2e given the design parameters.
Using the index of refraction of silica to estimate the optical wavevector difference between 1500 and 1600 nm, a 1 mm path length will produce a phase difference of 2*pi*(1.4446-1.443)*(1 mm)/(1550 nm) = 6.5 rad over this range. A 25 cm path length would produce a phase difference of ~1600 rad. Within one operation band, we probably need the phase to vary by ~1 rad or less over the bandwidth, so for the 25 cm device that might mean that the actual continuous bandwidth we can operate over at once is on the rough order of 1/16 nm. This is certainly more wideband than many resonant devices, but is quite narrowband compared to many other AOM demonstrations. The other recent work in [31] does achieve broad bandwidth because it consists of a single travelling-wave modulator, by comparison.
This analysis is of course somewhat speculative and based mostly on back-of-the-envelope math and prior published work, but in any case, the characterization of device performance as a function of wavelength is currently inadequate to support any claims of bandwidth at all.
It also makes me worry that some of the other assertions that are so confidently made in the paper may not have actually been fully thought through. It does not mean that the results are not interesting, but if it is difficult to produce a device for operation at a specific wavelength without extensive trial and error, then the results may not be too practical.
The tone and writing style of the paper is also at times quite stiff--many paragraphs are just a series of terse declarative sentences, without relationships or connections explained between them. Numerous sentences in a row start with "The" at several points in the paper, and some statements seem like non sequiturs.
I apologize for the harsh review, as the work is technologically impressive and it's clear that a lot of thought and hard work went into it. I just do not think the experimental data presented justify all of the claims made, particularly based on prior literature, and that a more detailed experimental investigation is warranted. I would love to be proven wrong, but I'm worried that the data presented do not tell the full story.
Some other minor comments are enumerated below:
1. It would be better to have a theoretical line plotted behind the data in Fig. 2f, instead of a random linear fit. In addition, the phrase "Indeed, the linear trend does continue with the experimentally collected data in Figure 2f" does not really mean anything. A linear increase does not "validate" the design methodology. A linear fit can have a slope of zero. Basically any curve is linear if you zoom in enough. A linear fit where 10 segments has 10x the modulation index of 1 segment, and where 30 segments have 30x the modulation index of 1 segment and 3x the modulation index of 10 segments, would validate the design methodology. Anything else is a false conclusion.
2. On page 3, the listing of equations (2-6) seems a bit awkward, since none of them are really motivated from theory or the text, or cited with references to the supplement or whatever, besides the reference for "coherence length" which is a bit of an interesting definition and might merit a bit more description to the reader in terms of what it actually means for this study.
3. On line 284, the phrase "The key to large transducers is to thicken the bus bars," does not really mean anything. It'd be better to say that adding thick bus bars lower resistance to improve impedance matching.
4. On line 365, I think that the phase matching technique does not seem as "completely novel" as the authors claim. The use of a spiral waveguide to enhance efficiency is not new, and in a bunch of the silicon a-o work, phase matching is explored in great detail. The arc length calculation for the bends is neat, but depending on fabrication tolerances it may not be required at that precision.
5. In the phrase "Insertion loss can be driven down further through removal of the AlN above the waveguides and recovering the foundry loss [56]," what does recovering mean? I thought losses were dominated by the Mo metal layer? Do you mean that the Mo and AlN could be deposited only in specific areas via a mask or liftoff, and that would make the insertion losses lower, similar to the best foundry values? I wonder if that might be a bit more feasible than removing it if it's already on top of the oxide clad.
6. The following sentences are somewhat incorrect: "The acousto-optic nature of the interaction can be seen by examining the slope of modulation efficiency for the 1st and 2nd order sidebands in response to an RF power sweep, shown in Figure 2h. The first and second sidebands scale with 1× and 2× the applied RF power in dBm." The modulation efficiency slopes do not say anything at all about the interaction being acousto-optic. Those power laws are the same for all linear sinusoidal modulation in all systems. It suggests that you are seeing phase modulation as expected. Saying the sidebands scale with 1x and 2x the power in dBm is true, but it's probably more correct to say that the first and second sideband powers scale linearly and quadratically with the applied RF power, in accordance with the expected trend (from the Jacobi–Anger Bessel expansion).

In any case, subject-verb agreement would dictate "photonics are." The phrase "They are cored down" I assume is of course referring to the processed wafers, but based on the sentence structure it would be referring to the photonics themselves, not the wafers, when the wafers are what are being cut down. ### Reviewer 1

The manuscript "Broadband acousto-optic modulators on Silicon Nitride" describes the development and implementation of a novel, traveling wave optically broadband acousto-optic modulator using thin silicon nitride waveguides. These modulators, capable of achieving a π/2 phase shift at a wavelength of 1550 nm, offer significant advantages due to their avoidance of complex fabrication processes and heterogeneous integration, capitalizing instead on ultra-low-loss waveguides to achieve long interaction lengths necessary for efficient modulation. The architecture utilizes spiraling waveguides that allow light to repeatedly pass through an acoustic field up to 38 times within a compact area, facilitating effective modulation with a Vπ of 8.98 V at 704 MHz and an insertion loss of just 1.13 dB. This manuscript also highlights the modulators' immediate applicability in optomechanical sensing systems. I recommend publication of this manuscript with a few minor comments:
1. In the abstract, “As silicon nitride has favorable optical properties, such as ultra-low-loss and a large optical transparency window, a rich ecosystem of potential photonic integrated circuits are therefore inhibited.” This sentence does not read well.
2. Figure 1, green, yellow, gray, materials not specified in figure or caption. From the text later one can sort of figure it out, but I recommend labeling those materials in the figure.
3. On phase matching, it mentions the basic idea of that in the text when introducing Figure 1e, and the results of increasing of numbers of loops in Figure 2. Could the author show more intermediate results in between of the design philosophy and final results? This is very important technical content for readers to understand, appreciate, and repeat the design.
4. The authors mention the loss of 1.1 dB is primarily because of metal layer; can they explain more how they reach this conclusion?
5. Could the authors provide more information regarding the material properties and method for AlN and Mo?
6. Could the authors comment on how to further how to further increase the acoustic-optical interaction in the future?

### Reviewer 2

The article under review describes broadband acousto-optic modulators on silicon nitride. In this work, the authors utilize ultra-low loss thin silicon nitride (<100nm) to realize the modulators. The modulator design is optimized by maximizing the optical and acoustic interaction through the use of a long spiral. This device avails modulators to the SiN photonics toolkit. The manuscript is interesting and I recommend publishing the manuscript after addressing the following points:
1) Integrated photonics technologies have a variety of modulator types (eg. electro-optic, free-carrier based). The modulator described in this work uses the acousto-optic effect. A table which allows a comparison of modulator merics such as half wave voltage / bandwidth / loss/ foot print etc. should be added to the paper.
2) Currently, the half wave voltage in the paper is higher than other technologies. Can the authors discuss what can be done to reduce it? The interaction length through ultra-low loss silicon nitride requires a 26cm length. There should be a fundamental limit to how long the waveguide can be that is loss limited. Can the authors comment on whether increasing the length is a feasible approach to reduce Vpi
3) Within the context of comment (2), there should be a trade off with the modulator footprint which may be useful to discuss as well.
4) Other than in Fig. 8 (d), can the authors comment on whether any data averaging was done to obtain the plots in the article? If so, how did they decide on the number of measurements used for the averaging?
5) To further improve the transducer, a greater thickness is required. More commentary around potential design improvements to enhance the modulator performance is warranted given that LiNbO3 modulators are currently very competitive. For example (but not limited to these), can the overlap be improved, and if so how much, could any other material integration give better performance etc.
6) Though higher order acoustic modes may be advantageous, it is not clear how one can control which modes are excited. The authors should clarify this. ### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, the authors demonstrate an acousto-optic phase modulator based on a spiral waveguide in thin-film silicon nitride, using travelling acoustic waves from IDTs on a Mo/AlN top layer. In contrast to prior work on silicon nitride, this modulator design does not use optical resonant enhancement, or suspended structures as in other recent work [31]. Using up to a 26 cm spiral waveguide, along with careful phase control over dozens of segments in the acoustic wave path, a V_pi of ~9 V is achieved for acousto-optic phase modulation at 704 MHz with ~1.1 dB insertion loss.
In general the work is interesting and seems technically to mostly be of high quality, except for a key issue addressed below. That aside, I am a bit uncertain if the manuscript represents the degree of novelty that the authors seem to claim, in part because the design is primarily based on principles that have already been reported in other recent work, and otherwise because I have some doubts about the applicability and practicality of using such a large structure and high RF power for producing phase modulation at a single RF frequency, particularly related to the next point:
Critically, I am not certain that I believe the authors' claim that the device is "broadband." It certainly is not broadband in the RF/acoustic sense, and I do not think it is broadband in the optical sense as well. When two (or more) modulators at the same frequency are placed in series, there can be constructive or destructive interference of the modulation index depending on the phase delay. The authors explore this in the supplement, and use this to design specific delay lengths between each segment. However I am not sure that their conclusion of the negligible impact of group index. Perhaps this can be true for operation around a certain theoretical design wavelength, but I do not see how this can produce broadband operation over 100+ nm. In any case, much more narrowband/continuous wavelength data would be needed to be provided to justify any claim about bandwidth.
I am not certain that the level of lithographic control to match phase delays to sub-radian levels over centimeter lengths is possible without post-fabrication trimming, due to variations in waveguide width and film stress and thickness across the wafer. However, perhaps given the weak confinement of thin silicon nitride waveguides and the use of a foundry process, this is possible in principle.
Even if constructive interference between all the segments is achieved, then it is still achieved for only certain wavelength bands due to material and waveguide dispersion. This is understood from basic modulator theory. If you have two modulators in series so that there is a phase difference theta between them:
phi(t) = beta*cos(omega*t) + beta*cos(omega*t+theta)
then this can be rewritten as
phi(t) = 2*beta*cos(theta/2)*cos(omega*t+theta/2).
If the phase theta is pi between the two modulation segments, then the modulation cancels. So, we want to keep theta to a multiple of 2*pi. This can be achieved, but it cannot be entirely "broadband" unless phi doesn't vary as a function of wavelength. I have a hard time believing that v_g varies so little over 100 nm that light does not accumulate an appreciable phase difference over tens of cm.
In the case of multiple segments, the interference becomes more complicated, but the principle is the same. Even with random phases between each segment, it should be possible to find "good" wavelengths where most of the interference is constructive. Conversely, there are "bad' wavelengths where most of the interference is destructive. This is already reported in detail in many papers, e.g. [33] and [37]. Another way of thinking about it is that, from the standpoint of light waves, experiencing many discrete modulation segments in series is not temporally very different from experiencing modulation at a discrete point in a resonator that it traverses numerous times, except that phase matching is more perfectly achieved for the latter via the resonance condition.
As far as I can tell, the only figure in the entire paper that is used to justify the claim of optical bandwidth is Fig. 2g, which shows modulation data at a series of coarse, discrete points across 100 nm. The same plot could be constructed from measurements of modulation in a resonator, as long as the laser was tuned to the resonant frequencies (equivalent to "good wavelengths" mentioned above). So in that sense the resonator approach would also seem to meet the authors' criterion for "broadband."
If the authors are not able to experimentally demonstrate broadband operation over a continuous wavelength band that contradicts this assessment, then the results of this paper are all a bit hard to interpret--since V_pi is going to vary as a function of wavelength, and the result of 9 V may occur only at certain magic wavelengths. I do think that the device may be able to achieve "broadband" operation over smaller continuous bands, but I believe that it cannot be continuously broadband over the 100 nm band shown in Fig. 2e given the design parameters.
Using the index of refraction of silica to estimate the optical wavevector difference between 1500 and 1600 nm, a 1 mm path length will produce a phase difference of 2*pi*(1.4446-1.443)*(1 mm)/(1550 nm) = 6.5 rad over this range. A 25 cm path length would produce a phase difference of ~1600 rad. Within one operation band, we probably need the phase to vary by ~1 rad or less over the bandwidth, so for the 25 cm device that might mean that the actual continuous bandwidth we can operate over at once is on the rough order of 1/16 nm. This is certainly more wideband than many resonant devices, but is quite narrowband compared to many other AOM demonstrations. The other recent work in [31] does achieve broad bandwidth because it consists of a single travelling-wave modulator, by comparison.
This analysis is of course somewhat speculative and based mostly on back-of-the-envelope math and prior published work, but in any case, the characterization of device performance as a function of wavelength is currently inadequate to support any claims of bandwidth at all.
It also makes me worry that some of the other assertions that are so confidently made in the paper may not have actually been fully thought through. It does not mean that the results are not interesting, but if it is difficult to produce a device for operation at a specific wavelength without extensive trial and error, then the results may not be too practical.
The tone and writing style of the paper is also at times quite stiff--many paragraphs are just a series of terse declarative sentences, without relationships or connections explained between them. Numerous sentences in a row start with "The" at several points in the paper, and some statements seem like non sequiturs.
I apologize for the harsh review, as the work is technologically impressive and it's clear that a lot of thought and hard work went into it. I just do not think the experimental data presented justify all of the claims made, particularly based on prior literature, and that a more detailed experimental investigation is warranted. I would love to be proven wrong, but I'm worried that the data presented do not tell the full story.
Some other minor comments are enumerated below:
1. It would be better to have a theoretical line plotted behind the data in Fig. 2f, instead of a random linear fit. In addition, the phrase "Indeed, the linear trend does continue with the experimentally collected data in Figure 2f" does not really mean anything. A linear increase does not "validate" the design methodology. A linear fit can have a slope of zero. Basically any curve is linear if you zoom in enough. A linear fit where 10 segments has 10x the modulation index of 1 segment, and where 30 segments have 30x the modulation index of 1 segment and 3x the modulation index of 10 segments, would validate the design methodology. Anything else is a false conclusion.
2. On page 3, the listing of equations (2-6) seems a bit awkward, since none of them are really motivated from theory or the text, or cited with references to the supplement or whatever, besides the reference for "coherence length" which is a bit of an interesting definition and might merit a bit more description to the reader in terms of what it actually means for this study.
3. On line 284, the phrase "The key to large transducers is to thicken the bus bars," does not really mean anything. It'd be better to say that adding thick bus bars lower resistance to improve impedance matching.
4. On line 365, I think that the phase matching technique does not seem as "completely novel" as the authors claim. The use of a spiral waveguide to enhance efficiency is not new, and in a bunch of the silicon a-o work, phase matching is explored in great detail. The arc length calculation for the bends is neat, but depending on fabrication tolerances it may not be required at that precision.
5. In the phrase "Insertion loss can be driven down further through removal of the AlN above the waveguides and recovering the foundry loss [56]," what does recovering mean? I thought losses were dominated by the Mo metal layer? Do you mean that the Mo and AlN could be deposited only in specific areas via a mask or liftoff, and that would make the insertion losses lower, similar to the best foundry values? I wonder if that might be a bit more feasible than removing it if it's already on top of the oxide clad.
6. The following sentences are somewhat incorrect: "The acousto-optic nature of the interaction can be seen by examining the slope of modulation efficiency for the 1st and 2nd order sidebands in response to an RF power sweep, shown in Figure 2h. The first and second sidebands scale with 1× and 2× the applied RF power in dBm." The modulation efficiency slopes do not say anything at all about the interaction being acousto-optic. Those power laws are the same for all linear sinusoidal modulation in all systems. It suggests that you are seeing phase modulation as expected. Saying the sidebands scale with 1x and 2x the power in dBm is true, but it's probably more correct to say that the first and second sideband powers scale linearly and quadratically with the applied RF power, in accordance with the expected trend (from the Jacobi–Anger Bessel expansion).
Some more line edits...
7. Line 219 page 4 - "coherent modulation" might not be the most descriptive term, since it's specifically interference between the modulation in the different segments that creates the peaks and nulls, I believe?
8. "The photonics is fabricated at a commercial foundry on 200 mm wafers. They are cored down to 100 mm and..." Using "photonics" in this way is a bit unusual, in part because I'd consider the entire device part of the photonics, not just the passive waveguides. In any case, subject-verb agreement would dictate "photonics are." The phrase "They are cored down" I assume is of course referring to the processed wafers, but based on the sentence structure it would be referring to the photonics themselves, not the wafers, when the wafers are what are being cut down. It would also be helpful to readers to mention which foundry process if that's not proprietary.
9. "fabricated on a foundry SiN photonics process to increase the acousto-optic interaction length in a compact area." Interjecting the foundry process here again makes it sound like that is the part that increases the interaction length. We already know it is from a foundry process since that was mentioned in the prior paragraph. If it is to be included, that phrase should be between commas here. Later in this paragraph you refer to this approach as "novel," which I am not sure is so true any there are several works that have introduced similar multi-pass designs.

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript "Broadband acousto-optic modulators on Silicon Nitride" describes the development and implementation of a novel, traveling wave optically broadband acousto-optic modulator using thin silicon nitride waveguides. These modulators, capable of achieving a π/2 phase shift at a wavelength of 1550 nm, offer significant advantages due to their avoidance of complex fabrication processes and heterogeneous integration, capitalizing instead on ultra-low-loss waveguides to achieve long interaction lengths necessary for efficient modulation. The architecture utilizes spiraling waveguides that allow light to repeatedly pass through an acoustic field up to 38 times within a compact area, facilitating effective modulation with a Vπ of 8.98 V at 704 MHz and an insertion loss of just 1.13 dB. This manuscript also highlights the modulators' immediate applicability in optomechanical sensing systems. I recommend publication of this manuscript with a few minor comments:
1. In the abstract, “As silicon nitride has favorable optical properties, such as ultra-low-loss and a large optical transparency window, a rich ecosystem of potential photonic integrated circuits are therefore inhibited.” This sentence does not read well.
2. Figure 1, green, yellow, gray, materials not specified in figure or caption. From the text later one can sort of figure it out, but I recommend labeling those materials in the figure.
3. On phase matching, it mentions the basic idea of that in the text when introducing Figure 1e, and the results of increasing of numbers of loops in Figure 2. Could the author show more intermediate results in between of the design philosophy and final results? This is very important technical content for readers to understand, appreciate, and repeat the design.
4. The authors mention the loss of 1.1 dB is primarily because of metal layer; can they explain more how they reach this conclusion?
5. Could the authors provide more information regarding the material properties and method for AlN and Mo?
6. Could the authors comment on how to further how to further increase the acoustic-optical interaction in the future?

### Reviewer 2

The article under review describes broadband acousto-optic modulators on silicon nitride. In this work, the authors utilize ultra-low loss thin silicon nitride (<100nm) to realize the modulators. The modulator design is optimized by maximizing the optical and acoustic interaction through the use of a long spiral. This device avails modulators to the SiN photonics toolkit. The manuscript is interesting and I recommend publishing the manuscript after addressing the following points:
1) Integrated photonics technologies have a variety of modulator types (eg. electro-optic, free-carrier based). The modulator described in this work uses the acousto-optic effect. A table which allows a comparison of modulator merics such as half wave voltage / bandwidth / loss/ foot print etc. should be added to the paper.
2) Currently, the half wave voltage in the paper is higher than other technologies. Can the authors discuss what can be done to reduce it? The interaction length through ultra-low loss silicon nitride requires a 26cm length. There should be a fundamental limit to how long the waveguide can be that is loss limited. Can the authors comment on whether increasing the length is a feasible approach to reduce Vpi
3) Within the context of comment (2), there should be a trade off with the modulator footprint which may be useful to discuss as well.
4) Other than in Fig. 8 (d), can the authors comment on whether any data averaging was done to obtain the plots in the article? If so, how did they decide on the number of measurements used for the averaging?
5) To further improve the transducer, a greater thickness is required. More commentary around potential design improvements to enhance the modulator performance is warranted given that LiNbO3 modulators are currently very competitive. For example (but not limited to these), can the overlap be improved, and if so how much, could any other material integration give better performance etc.
6) Though higher order acoustic modes may be advantageous, it is not clear how one can control which modes are excited. The authors should clarify this. If there is a difficulty in exciting a specific higher order mode and the design is typically optimized for a specific mode, then is there an inherent tradeoff?

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, the authors demonstrate an acousto-optic phase modulator based on a spiral waveguide in thin-film silicon nitride, using travelling acoustic waves from IDTs on a Mo/AlN top layer. In contrast to prior work on silicon nitride, this modulator design does not use optical resonant enhancement, or suspended structures as in other recent work [31]. Using up to a 26 cm spiral waveguide, along with careful phase control over dozens of segments in the acoustic wave path, a V_pi of ~9 V is achieved for acousto-optic phase modulation at 704 MHz with ~1.1 dB insertion loss.
In general the work is interesting and seems technically to mostly be of high quality, except for a key issue addressed below. That aside, I am a bit uncertain if the manuscript represents the degree of novelty that the authors seem to claim, in part because the design is primarily based on principles that have already been reported in other recent work, and otherwise because I have some doubts about the applicability and practicality of using such a large structure and high RF power for producing phase modulation at a single RF frequency, particularly related to the next point:
Critically, I am not certain that I believe the authors' claim that the device is "broadband." It certainly is not broadband in the RF/acoustic sense, and I do not think it is broadband in the optical sense as well. When two (or more) modulators at the same frequency are placed in series, there can be constructive or destructive interference of the modulation index depending on the phase delay. The authors explore this in the supplement, and use this to design specific delay lengths between each segment. However I am not sure that their conclusion of the negligible impact of group index. Perhaps this can be true for operation around a certain theoretical design wavelength, but I do not see how this can produce broadband operation over 100+ nm. In any case, much more narrowband/continuous wavelength data would be needed to be provided to justify any claim about bandwidth.
I am not certain that the level of lithographic control to match phase delays to sub-radian levels over centimeter lengths is possible without post-fabrication trimming, due to variations in waveguide width and film stress and thickness across the wafer. However, perhaps given the weak confinement of thin silicon nitride waveguides and the use of a foundry process, this is possible in principle.
Even if constructive interference between all the segments is achieved, then it is still achieved for only certain wavelength bands due to material and waveguide dispersion. This is understood from basic modulator theory. If you have two modulators in series so that there is a phase difference theta between them:
phi(t) = beta*cos(omega*t) + beta*cos(omega*t+theta)
then this can be rewritten as
phi(t) = 2*beta*cos(theta/2)*cos(omega*t+theta/2).
If the phase theta is pi between the two modulation segments, then the modulation cancels. So, we want to keep theta to a multiple of 2*pi. This can be achieved, but it cannot be entirely "broadband" unless phi doesn't vary as a function of wavelength. I have a hard time believing that v_g varies so little over 100 nm that light does not accumulate an appreciable phase difference over tens of cm.
In the case of multiple segments, the interference becomes more complicated, but the principle is the same. Even with random phases between each segment, it should be possible to find "good" wavelengths where most of the interference is constructive. Conversely, there are "bad' wavelengths where most of the interference is destructive. This is already reported in detail in many papers, e.g. [33] and [37]. Another way of thinking about it is that, from the standpoint of light waves, experiencing many discrete modulation segments in series is not temporally very different from experiencing modulation at a discrete point in a resonator that it traverses numerous times, except that phase matching is more perfectly achieved for the latter via the resonance condition.
As far as I can tell, the only figure in the entire paper that is used to justify the claim of optical bandwidth is Fig. 2g, which shows modulation data at a series of coarse, discrete points across 100 nm. The same plot could be constructed from measurements of modulation in a resonator, as long as the laser was tuned to the resonant frequencies (equivalent to "good wavelengths" mentioned above). So in that sense the resonator approach would also seem to meet the authors' criterion for "broadband."
If the authors are not able to experimentally demonstrate broadband operation over a continuous wavelength band that contradicts this assessment, then the results of this paper are all a bit hard to interpret--since V_pi is going to vary as a function of wavelength, and the result of 9 V may occur only at certain magic wavelengths. I do think that the device may be able to achieve "broadband" operation over smaller continuous bands, but I believe that it cannot be continuously broadband over the 100 nm band shown in Fig. 2e given the design parameters.
Using the index of refraction of silica to estimate the optical wavevector difference between 1500 and 1600 nm, a 1 mm path length will produce a phase difference of 2*pi*(1.4446-1.443)*(1 mm)/(1550 nm) = 6.5 rad over this range. A 25 cm path length would produce a phase difference of ~1600 rad. Within one operation band, we probably need the phase to vary by ~1 rad or less over the bandwidth, so for the 25 cm device that might mean that the actual continuous bandwidth we can operate over at once is on the rough order of 1/16 nm. This is certainly more wideband than many resonant devices, but is quite narrowband compared to many other AOM demonstrations. The other recent work in [31] does achieve broad bandwidth because it consists of a single travelling-wave modulator, by comparison.
This analysis is of course somewhat speculative and based mostly on back-of-the-envelope math and prior published work, but in any case, the characterization of device performance as a function of wavelength is currently inadequate to support any claims of bandwidth at all.
It also makes me worry that some of the other assertions that are so confidently made in the paper may not have actually been fully thought through. It does not mean that the results are not interesting, but if it is difficult to produce a device for operation at a specific wavelength without extensive trial and error, then the results may not be too practical.
The tone and writing style of the paper is also at times quite stiff--many paragraphs are just a series of terse declarative sentences, without relationships or connections explained between them. Numerous sentences in a row start with "The" at several points in the paper, and some statements seem like non sequiturs.
I apologize for the harsh review, as the work is technologically impressive and it's clear that a lot of thought and hard work went into it. I just do not think the experimental data presented justify all of the claims made, particularly based on prior literature, and that a more detailed experimental investigation is warranted. I would love to be proven wrong, but I'm worried that the data presented do not tell the full story.
Some other minor comments are enumerated below:
1. It would be better to have a theoretical line plotted behind the data in Fig. 2f, instead of a random linear fit. In addition, the phrase "Indeed, the linear trend does continue with the experimentally collected data in Figure 2f" does not really mean anything. A linear increase does not "validate" the design methodology. A linear fit can have a slope of zero. Basically any curve is linear if you zoom in enough. A linear fit where 10 segments has 10x the modulation index of 1 segment, and where 30 segments have 30x the modulation index of 1 segment and 3x the modulation index of 10 segments, would validate the design methodology. Anything else is a false conclusion.
2. On page 3, the listing of equations (2-6) seems a bit awkward, since none of them are really motivated from theory or the text, or cited with references to the supplement or whatever, besides the reference for "coherence length" which is a bit of an interesting definition and might merit a bit more description to the reader in terms of what it actually means for this study.
3. On line 284, the phrase "The key to large transducers is to thicken the bus bars," does not really mean anything. It'd be better to say that adding thick bus bars lower resistance to improve impedance matching.
4. On line 365, I think that the phase matching technique does not seem as "completely novel" as the authors claim. The use of a spiral waveguide to enhance efficiency is not new, and in a bunch of the silicon a-o work, phase matching is explored in great detail. The arc length calculation for the bends is neat, but depending on fabrication tolerances it may not be required at that precision.
5. In the phrase "Insertion loss can be driven down further through removal of the AlN above the waveguides and recovering the foundry loss [56]," what does recovering mean? I thought losses were dominated by the Mo metal layer? Do you mean that the Mo and AlN could be deposited only in specific areas via a mask or liftoff, and that would make the insertion losses lower, similar to the best foundry values? I wonder if that might be a bit more feasible than removing it if it's already on top of the oxide clad.
6. The following sentences are somewhat incorrect: "The acousto-optic nature of the interaction can be seen by examining the slope of modulation efficiency for the 1st and 2nd order sidebands in response to an RF power sweep, shown in Figure 2h. The first and second sidebands scale with 1× and 2× the applied RF power in dBm." The modulation efficiency slopes do not say anything at all about the interaction being acousto-optic. Those power laws are the same for all linear sinusoidal modulation in all systems. It suggests that you are seeing phase modulation as expected. Saying the sidebands scale with 1x and 2x the power in dBm is true, but it's probably more correct to say that the first and second sideband powers scale linearly and quadratically with the applied RF power, in accordance with the expected trend (from the Jacobi–Anger Bessel expansion).
Some more line edits...
7. Line 219 page 4 - "coherent modulation" might not be the most descriptive term, since it's specifically interference between the modulation in the different segments that creates the peaks and nulls, I believe?
8. "The photonics is fabricated at a commercial foundry on 200 mm wafers. They are cored down to 100 mm and..." Using "photonics" in this way is a bit unusual, in part because I'd consider the entire device part of the photonics, not just the passive waveguides. In any case, subject-verb agreement would dictate "photonics are." The phrase "They are cored down" I assume is of course referring to the processed wafers, but based on the sentence structure it would be referring to the photonics themselves, not the wafers, when the wafers are what are being cut down. It would also be helpful to readers to mention which foundry process if that's not proprietary.
9. "fabricated on a foundry SiN photonics process to increase the acousto-optic interaction length in a compact area." Interjecting the foundry process here again makes it sound like that is the part that increases the interaction length. We already know it is from a foundry process since that was mentioned in the prior paragraph. If it is to be included, that phrase should be between commas here. Later in this paragraph you refer to this approach as "novel," which I am not sure is so true any there are several works that have introduced similar multi-pass designs.

The manuscript "Broadband acousto-optic modulators on Silicon Nitride" describes the development and implementation of a novel, traveling wave optically broadband acousto-optic modulator using thin silicon nitride waveguides. These modulators, capable of achieving a π/2 phase shift at a wavelength of 1550 nm, offer significant advantages due to their avoidance of complex fabrication processes and heterogeneous integration, capitalizing instead on ultra-low-loss waveguides to achieve long interaction lengths necessary for efficient modulation. The architecture utilizes spiraling waveguides that allow light to repeatedly pass through an acoustic field up to 38 times within a compact area, facilitating effective modulation with a Vπ of 8.98 V at 704 MHz and an insertion loss of just 1.13 dB. This manuscript also highlights the modulators' immediate applicability in optomechanical sensing systems. I recommend publication of this manuscript with a few minor comments:
1. In the abstract, “As silicon nitride has favorable optical properties, such as ultra-low-loss and a large optical transparency window, a rich ecosystem of potential photonic integrated circuits are therefore inhibited.” This sentence does not read well.
2. Figure 1, green, yellow, gray, materials not specified in figure or caption. From the text later one can sort of figure it out, but I recommend labeling those materials in the figure.
3. On phase matching, it mentions the basic idea of that in the text when introducing Figure 1e, and the results of increasing of numbers of loops in Figure 2. Could the author show more intermediate results in between of the design philosophy and final results? This is very important technical content for readers to understand, appreciate, and repeat the design.
4. The authors mention the loss of 1.1 dB is primarily because of metal layer; can they explain more how they reach this conclusion?
5. Could the authors provide more information regarding the material properties and method for AlN and Mo?
6. Could the authors comment on how to further how to further increase the acoustic-optical interaction in the future?

### Reviewer 2

The article under review describes broadband acousto-optic modulators on silicon nitride. In this work, the authors utilize ultra-low loss thin silicon nitride (<100nm) to realize the modulators. The modulator design is optimized by maximizing the optical and acoustic interaction through the use of a long spiral. This device avails modulators to the SiN photonics toolkit. The manuscript is interesting and I recommend publishing the manuscript after addressing the following points:
1) Integrated photonics technologies have a variety of modulator types (eg. electro-optic, free-carrier based). The modulator described in this work uses the acousto-optic effect. A table which allows a comparison of modulator merics such as half wave voltage / bandwidth / loss/ foot print etc. should be added to the paper.
2) Currently, the half wave voltage in the paper is higher than other technologies. Can the authors discuss what can be done to reduce it? The interaction length through ultra-low loss silicon nitride requires a 26cm length. There should be a fundamental limit to how long the waveguide can be that is loss limited. Can the authors comment on whether increasing the length is a feasible approach to reduce Vpi
3) Within the context of comment (2), there should be a trade off with the modulator footprint which may be useful to discuss as well.
4) Other than in Fig. 8 (d), can the authors comment on whether any data averaging was done to obtain the plots in the article? If so, how did they decide on the number of measurements used for the averaging?
5) To further improve the transducer, a greater thickness is required. More commentary around potential design improvements to enhance the modulator performance is warranted given that LiNbO3 modulators are currently very competitive. For example (but not limited to these), can the overlap be improved, and if so how much, could any other material integration give better performance etc.
6) Though higher order acoustic modes may be advantageous, it is not clear how one can control which modes are excited. The authors should clarify this. If there is a difficulty in exciting a specific higher order mode and the design is typically optimized for a specific mode, then is there an inherent tradeoff?

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, the authors demonstrate an acousto-optic phase modulator based on a spiral waveguide in thin-film silicon nitride, using travelling acoustic waves from IDTs on a Mo/AlN top layer. In contrast to prior work on silicon nitride, this modulator design does not use optical resonant enhancement, or suspended structures as in other recent work [31]. Using up to a 26 cm spiral waveguide, along with careful phase control over dozens of segments in the acoustic wave path, a V_pi of ~9 V is achieved for acousto-optic phase modulation at 704 MHz with ~1.1 dB insertion loss.
In general the work is interesting and seems technically to mostly be of high quality, except for a key issue addressed below. That aside, I am a bit uncertain if the manuscript represents the degree of novelty that the authors seem to claim, in part because the design is primarily based on principles that have already been reported in other recent work, and otherwise because I have some doubts about the applicability and practicality of using such a large structure and high RF power for producing phase modulation at a single RF frequency, particularly related to the next point:
Critically, I am not certain that I believe the authors' claim that the device is "broadband." It certainly is not broadband in the RF/acoustic sense, and I do not think it is broadband in the optical sense as well. When two (or more) modulators at the same frequency are placed in series, there can be constructive or destructive interference of the modulation index depending on the phase delay. The authors explore this in the supplement, and use this to design specific delay lengths between each segment. However I am not sure that their conclusion of the negligible impact of group index. Perhaps this can be true for operation around a certain theoretical design wavelength, but I do not see how this can produce broadband operation over 100+ nm. In any case, much more narrowband/continuous wavelength data would be needed to be provided to justify any claim about bandwidth.
I am not certain that the level of lithographic control to match phase delays to sub-radian levels over centimeter lengths is possible without post-fabrication trimming, due to variations in waveguide width and film stress and thickness across the wafer. However, perhaps given the weak confinement of thin silicon nitride waveguides and the use of a foundry process, this is possible in principle.
Even if constructive interference between all the segments is achieved, then it is still achieved for only certain wavelength bands due to material and waveguide dispersion. This is understood from basic modulator theory. If you have two modulators in series so that there is a phase difference theta between them:
phi(t) = beta*cos(omega*t) + beta*cos(omega*t+theta)
then this can be rewritten as
phi(t) = 2*beta*cos(theta/2)*cos(omega*t+theta/2).
If the phase theta is pi between the two modulation segments, then the modulation cancels. So, we want to keep theta to a multiple of 2*pi. This can be achieved, but it cannot be entirely "broadband" unless phi doesn't vary as a function of wavelength. I have a hard time believing that v_g varies so little over 100 nm that light does not accumulate an appreciable phase difference over tens of cm.
In the case of multiple segments, the interference becomes more complicated, but the principle is the same. Even with random phases between each segment, it should be possible to find "good" wavelengths where most of the interference is constructive. Conversely, there are "bad' wavelengths where most of the interference is destructive. This is already reported in detail in many papers, e.g. [33] and [37]. Another way of thinking about it is that, from the standpoint of light waves, experiencing many discrete modulation segments in series is not temporally very different from experiencing modulation at a discrete point in a resonator that it traverses numerous times, except that phase matching is more perfectly achieved for the latter via the resonance condition.
As far as I can tell, the only figure in the entire paper that is used to justify the claim of optical bandwidth is Fig. 2g, which shows modulation data at a series of coarse, discrete points across 100 nm. The same plot could be constructed from measurements of modulation in a resonator, as long as the laser was tuned to the resonant frequencies (equivalent to "good wavelengths" mentioned above). So in that sense the resonator approach would also seem to meet the authors' criterion for "broadband."
If the authors are not able to experimentally demonstrate broadband operation over a continuous wavelength band that contradicts this assessment, then the results of this paper are all a bit hard to interpret--since V_pi is going to vary as a function of wavelength, and the result of 9 V may occur only at certain magic wavelengths. I do think that the device may be able to achieve "broadband" operation over smaller continuous bands, but I believe that it cannot be continuously broadband over the 100 nm band shown in Fig. 2e given the design parameters.
Using the index of refraction of silica to estimate the optical wavevector difference between 1500 and 1600 nm, a 1 mm path length will produce a phase difference of 2*pi*(1.4446-1.443)*(1 mm)/(1550 nm) = 6.5 rad over this range. A 25 cm path length would produce a phase difference of ~1600 rad. Within one operation band, we probably need the phase to vary by ~1 rad or less over the bandwidth, so for the 25 cm device that might mean that the actual continuous bandwidth we can operate over at once is on the rough order of 1/16 nm. This is certainly more wideband than many resonant devices, but is quite narrowband compared to many other AOM demonstrations. The other recent work in [31] does achieve broad bandwidth because it consists of a single travelling-wave modulator, by comparison.
This analysis is of course somewhat speculative and based mostly on back-of-the-envelope math and prior published work, but in any case, the characterization of device performance as a function of wavelength is currently inadequate to support any claims of bandwidth at all.
It also makes me worry that some of the other assertions that are so confidently made in the paper may not have actually been fully thought through. It does not mean that the results are not interesting, but if it is difficult to produce a device for operation at a specific wavelength without extensive trial and error, then the results may not be too practical.
The tone and writing style of the paper is also at times quite stiff--many paragraphs are just a series of terse declarative sentences, without relationships or connections explained between them. Numerous sentences in a row start with "The" at several points in the paper, and some statements seem like non sequiturs.
I apologize for the harsh review, as the work is technologically impressive and it's clear that a lot of thought and hard work went into it. I just do not think the experimental data presented justify all of the claims made, particularly based on prior literature, and that a more detailed experimental investigation is warranted. I would love to be proven wrong, but I'm worried that the data presented do not tell the full story.
Some other minor comments are enumerated below:
1. It would be better to have a theoretical line plotted behind the data in Fig. 2f, instead of a random linear fit. In addition, the phrase "Indeed, the linear trend does continue with the experimentally collected data in Figure 2f" does not really mean anything. A linear increase does not "validate" the design methodology. A linear fit can have a slope of zero. Basically any curve is linear if you zoom in enough. A linear fit where 10 segments has 10x the modulation index of 1 segment, and where 30 segments have 30x the modulation index of 1 segment and 3x the modulation index of 10 segments, would validate the design methodology. Anything else is a false conclusion.
2. On page 3, the listing of equations (2-6) seems a bit awkward, since none of them are really motivated from theory or the text, or cited with references to the supplement or whatever, besides the reference for "coherence length" which is a bit of an interesting definition and might merit a bit more description to the reader in terms of what it actually means for this study.
3. On line 284, the phrase "The key to large transducers is to thicken the bus bars," does not really mean anything. It'd be better to say that adding thick bus bars lower resistance to improve impedance matching.
4. On line 365, I think that the phase matching technique does not seem as "completely novel" as the authors claim. The use of a spiral waveguide to enhance efficiency is not new, and in a bunch of the silicon a-o work, phase matching is explored in great detail. The arc length calculation for the bends is neat, but depending on fabrication tolerances it may not be required at that precision.
5. In the phrase "Insertion loss can be driven down further through removal of the AlN above the waveguides and recovering the foundry loss [56]," what does recovering mean? I thought losses were dominated by the Mo metal layer? Do you mean that the Mo and AlN could be deposited only in specific areas via a mask or liftoff, and that would make the insertion losses lower, similar to the best foundry values? I wonder if that might be a bit more feasible than removing it if it's already on top of the oxide clad.
6. The following sentences are somewhat incorrect: "The acousto-optic nature of the interaction can be seen by examining the slope of modulation efficiency for the 1st and 2nd order sidebands in response to an RF power sweep, shown in Figure 2h. The first and second sidebands scale with 1× and 2× the applied RF power in dBm." The modulation efficiency slopes do not say anything at all about the interaction being acousto-optic. Those power laws are the same for all linear sinusoidal modulation in all systems. It suggests that you are seeing phase modulation as expected. Saying the sidebands scale with 1x and 2x the power in dBm is true, but it's probably more correct to say that the first and second sideband powers scale linearly and quadratically with the applied RF power, in accordance with the expected trend (from the Jacobi–Anger Bessel expansion).
Some more line edits...
7. Line 219 page 4 - "coherent modulation" might not be the most descriptive term, since it's specifically interference between the modulation in the different segments that creates the peaks and nulls, I believe?
8. "The photonics is fabricated at a commercial foundry on 200 mm wafers. They are cored down to 100 mm and..." Using "photonics" in this way is a bit unusual, in part because I'd consider the entire device part of the photonics, not just the passive waveguides. In any case, subject-verb agreement would dictate "photonics are." The phrase "They are cored down" I assume is of course referring to the processed wafers, but based on the sentence structure it would be referring to the photonics themselves, not the wafers, when the wafers are what are being cut down. It would also be helpful to readers to mention which foundry process if that's not proprietary.
9. "fabricated on a foundry SiN photonics process to increase the acousto-optic interaction length in a compact area." Interjecting the foundry process here again makes it sound like that is the part that increases the interaction length. We already know it is from a foundry process since that was mentioned in the prior paragraph. If it is to be included, that phrase should be between commas here. Later in this paragraph you refer to this approach as "novel," which I am not sure is so true any there are several works that have introduced similar multi-pass designs.
